explanation: Fires on function or connective words in formal, expository or boilerplate prose: 'referred[ to]', 'hereina[fter]', '[Such] apparatuses', 'INCLUDING,[ BUT] NOT LIMITED', '[Instead]', 'credits[ for]'. It also fires on scattered code and name tokens. No single lexical trigger links these, so it is hard to predict from the token alone.

A mixture with no shared trigger. Code tokens: assignment '=', 'from' in JS imports, 'require', 'range([0]'. License boilerplate: 'WITHOUT WARRANTIES', 'distributed with[ this]'. Country names after 'state/country of' ('India', 'USA'). Assorted prepositions and variables in prose and math.

A mixture. Fires on assignment '=' in PHP and Objective-C code, on periods and letters inside legal citations ('L. REV[.]', 'F.2[d]', 'No[.]'), on reference-tag suffixes ('microm[achines]'), and on various verbs and nouns in prose ('has', 'made', 'will', 'located'). There is no clear unifying context.

Several unrelated triggers: the word 'construction' (machinery, workers, sites); command-line option dashes ('ls[ -]la', 'nslookup[ -]q'); jQuery/Angular '$.' and '.$' tokens; format specifiers ('%'); assorted punctuation ('，', ':', '“'). These do not form one concept.

Monetary quantity: fires strongly on words for an amount of money ('amount', 'montant', 'Betrag', 'beløp', 'sum') and on 'in' right after a money figure ('$40 billion[ in] market value', '$11 million[ in] funding'). Fires more weakly on 'how[ much]' and currency pieces ('euro'). Unrelated tokens get near zero.

A mixture. Fires on commas in BSD/MIT license boilerplate ('source and binary forms[,]', 'Permission is hereby granted[,]') and on 'import[ com]' in Java imports. It also fires on many unrelated function words and digits in prose ('more', 'the', 'to', 'not', 'is', 'or'). No coherent trigger beyond the license commas.

Source code: fires on syntax tokens that link a name to its value or definition inside code. These include '=>' in PHP arrays, ':' after object keys before a function ('success[:] function'), '=' in 'module.exports =', quoted string arguments, and 'public' or indentation that starts a member declaration in a class. It fires weakly on other code tokens and not at all on prose.

A mixture. Fires on runs of punctuation characters or the word 'punctuation' itself, on regex escape sequences, on '"testing"' in Go imports, on 'Conditions' in 'Terms and Conditions', and on part numbers. It also fires on scattered prose words ('mean', 'root', 'Score', 'Gear'). No single theme.

Fires mostly on mid-sentence verbs, auxiliaries and prepositions in scientific, medical or encyclopedic prose ('can result', 'may[ appear]', 'are[ under] trials', 'lost[ in] the first round'). It also fires on drug or noun endings ('risperid[one]') and some code and price digits. No specific trigger is apparent.

Programming identifiers inside code or programming Q&A: fires on camelCase or PascalCase class, method and property names ('JsonObject', 'marginTop', 'IllegalArgumentException', 'managedObjectContext', 'DataTable') and on the '.googleapis' domain piece. It fires more weakly on Latin-derived technical word pieces in scientific prose.

Fires on the second, completing part of a fixed domain-specific compound term or name, mostly in technical, medical or business text: 'fill[ factor]', 'quantum[ efficiency]', 'cord[ blood]', 'below[ knee]', 'dividend[ yield]', 'Deepwater[ Horizon]', 'h[ant]avirus', 'Deloitte & Tou[che]'. A first word that does not complete such a term gets little activation.

Word-piece detector for 'olig'/'oblig' stems ('Oligosaccharides', 'Obligations', 'oligomers', 'obligate', 'oligarchy') and, more moderately, for the 'lation' piece of 'ablation'. It also fires weakly on other odd subword pieces in rare words.

Fires in scientific or medical text on modifiers that name the population or physical regime studied. Population: 'pediatric', 'adults', 'children', 'infants', 'aged [N]', '68-year old'. Regime: 'ultracold', 'high energy', 'accelerate' ions. These are two related kinds of study-scope qualifier.

Fires on a middle subword piece inside a rare proper name or abbreviation, most reliably 'At[ty]' in 'Atty. Gen.' / 'U.S. Atty.' lines of legal briefs. Other examples: 'Ro[que]', 'An[them]', 'Krasnooktyabrsk[oy]e', 'Kar[achi]', 'Act[in]'. Common whole words give weak or no activation.
